Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event
The same time of day the event occurred

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A medical-equipment visual trigger is hard to reconcile as a central combat-related trigger for this profile, especially alongside otherwise combat-consistent threat items and without any medical/hospital-related memory or appraisal content. It suggests a different trauma context and is clinically difficult to integrate with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense rage on recall conflicts with the paired reports of emotionally numb recall and the memory feeling alien/detached. Fluctuation can occur, but as a compact three-item profile these items pull in opposing directions—high emotional arousal versus marked dissociative detachment—without other memory content to bridge them.

Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Rage on Recall' conflicts with the paired endorsement of markedly detached recall ('Emotionless Recall' and 'Memory Feels Alien'). Intense rage during recall and recall experienced as numb/alien can both occur in PTSD, but selecting all three as coequal memory descriptors creates a direct within-node tension between highly affect-laden remembering and strongly depersonalized, affectless remembering. The rest of the profile coherently reflects severe combat-related PTSD, but this specific Memory combination is the main clinically questionable inconsistency.

issues.item: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, two items describe markedly detached/derealized recall ('emotionless', 'belongs to someone else') while another describes intensely affect-laden reliving ('same terror I felt at the time'). These can both occur across different moments in PTSD, but as the only three selected memory items they pull in opposing directions and are not a clean, internally coherent depiction of a single dominant memory style for this profile.

These two appraisals are plausible in severe PTSD, but for a 63-year-old married airline pilot they create a hard-to-explain mismatch with the rest of the profile when presented without any trauma-linked appraisal content. 'I have no future' is especially discordant for an older, still-employed patient and is not well integrated with the combat-specific trigger/threat pattern. The Negative Appraisals node is dominated by global depressive identity/future statements rather than trauma-related meanings that would plausibly connect to the very strong Triggers → Negative Appraisals edge in the formulation.

vignette:
At 63, Tane had built a life that looked disciplined and steady from the outside. He was an airline pilot, married, and used to moving through airports with the practiced calm of a man who had spent decades reading weather, altitude, and risk. But the event that later came to dominate his inner life belonged to an earlier chapter, during combat, when a helicopter’s arrival changed the air around him before he could fully register what was happening. He remembered the particular texture under his hand that day with a startling clarity, a coarse, gritty feel that still carried the force of the moment for him years later. It was the sort of detail he would not have expected to stay, yet it remained fixed, attached to the same hour of the day when the event had occurred, as if his body had kept its own clock for danger. At that time, the sound of helicopters or aircraft overhead was not just background noise but an immediate signal that something terrible could be about to unfold.

In the years that followed, Tane found that the memory did not sit comfortably in the past. When he tried to think about it, he felt as though it belonged to someone else, as if he were describing another man’s life rather than his own. That distance did not make it easier. If anything, it made the memory feel stranger, harder to place, and when it surfaced it brought back the same terror he had felt then, with none of the softening that time usually brings. He described how a sudden sound or an unexpected detail in his surroundings could bring the whole thing back without warning, full and immediate, as though the scene had opened in front of him again. A helicopter passing at the airport, or even the low mechanical chop of aircraft sound from elsewhere, could make his chest tighten and leave him momentarily caught between the present and that earlier battlefield. He did not need to be trying to remember; the memory would arrive on its own.

As those experiences accumulated, Tane became increasingly alert to signs of danger in daily life. He found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, and he said he had started to move through evenings with a kind of guarded patience, as if darkness made the world less trustworthy. He would check the doors and look out into the yard, not because he believed something was definitely there, but because being unprepared felt unbearable to him. When he entered a room or building, he automatically scanned for exits. This was true in hotels, in terminals, in unfamiliar offices, and even in places he knew well enough to name every corridor. The habit was so immediate that his wife had noticed it before he did; he would choose where to sit in a restaurant by what let him see the door, then settle only partly, still tracking movement around him. Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard. A person turning quickly, a hand lifting too fast, someone stepping into his path without warning—these were the moments that caught his attention and pulled him tight inside himself, as if his body had already decided that quick motion meant trouble.

Tane had also come to believe difficult things about himself and the world. He spoke with quiet certainty that there was something wrong with him as a person, not in a dramatic way but in the weary tone of someone who had been carrying that thought for a long time. He could remember being more open, more content, and said bluntly that he used to be a happy person but now was always miserable. That loss weighed on him because it felt like a permanent change, not a bad patch. Alongside that, he had developed a conviction that the world is a dangerous place. He did not say this with theatrical fear; rather, it came out as a fact he had learned the hard way and could not unlearn. The result was that ordinary settings never felt entirely ordinary. Even in his work as an airline pilot, where professionalism required composure and routine, he found himself noticing aircraft sounds with a tension that other people around him would not see. In airports and around the plane, he could feel himself monitoring his surroundings more than he wanted to admit.

What finally brought Tane to seek help was the exhaustion of living this way for so long and the strain it was placing on his marriage and his work life. He had tried to manage it quietly, but the constant vigilance, the intrusive returns of the memory, and the sense that he no longer recognized himself had become harder to contain. He was afraid that if nothing changed, he would continue shrinking his life around danger, always on guard, always bracing. What he hoped for was more modest than forgetting. He wanted to feel safe again at night, to enter a room without immediately searching for exits, and to be able to move through the world without every helicopter sound or sudden movement pulling him back into terror.
